title: Moving Around
summary: Walk through folders with cd, .. and ~, and find hidden files.
intro:
Folders can live inside other folders, like boxes inside boxes.
In this lesson you will walk into folders, climb back out, jump home, and discover a hidden file.
Watch the prompt: it always shows where you are standing. ~ means your home folder.
outro: You can now walk anywhere you like! cd, .., ~ and ls -a are your map and compass.

hints: cd means 'change directory'. After cd, write the name of the folder.
steps.explain: Look at the prompt: it now shows ~/school. You moved into the folder, like double-clicking it. Try ls to see what is inside.

steps.instruction: Now go one level deeper, into the folder math.
hints: You are already inside school, so you only need the name of the next folder.
steps.explain: A path like math is called relative: it starts from the folder where you are standing right now.

steps.instruction: Go back up one folder, to school.
hints: Two dots .. mean 'the folder above me' (the parent folder).
steps.explain: One dot . is the folder you are in. Two dots .. are the folder above it. cd ../.. would climb up two levels.

steps.instruction: Jump straight back to your home folder.
hints: The symbol ~ (tilde) means 'home'. And cd with nothing after it also goes home.
steps.explain: In Terminal Academy, home (~) is your sandbox. In a real terminal, ~ is your own user folder, like /Users/ank on a Mac or /home/ank on Linux.

steps.instruction: A file is hiding here! Show ALL files, also the hidden ones.
hints: Plain ls does not show hidden files. ls has an option -a, which means 'all'.
steps.explain: Files whose name starts with a dot (.) are hidden. Settings files are often hidden, so they don't clutter your folders. You also see . and .. in the list. Read the note with cat .secret_note.txt if you like!

steps.instruction: Go into the folder school/art with ONE command.
hints: You can join folder names with a slash /.
steps.explain: A path that starts with / is absolute: it starts at the very top of the computer, like /Users or /home. A path without / at the start is relative. Pro tip for real terminals: type the first letters and press Tab, and the shell completes the name for you.
